title: validate_nested relies on ModelConfig.__post_init__ for head alignment but does not assert it for the variant
description: validate_nested deliberately omits an n_heads / head-alignment check (comment at 235-237) on the grounds that head_dim*n_heads==d_model is already a ModelConfig invariant. This is correct as long as every variant_cfg reaching sliced() is a genuine ModelConfig instance (which __post_init__ has validated). It holds today because model.sliced(supernet_model, variant_cfg: ModelConfig) only ever receives ModelConfig instances. The latent fragility is that the whole-head-alignment guarantee for the *slice* is enforced one layer away from where the slice is taken; if anything ever constructed a partial/raw-dim slice path bypassing ModelConfig, the [:dv] slice could land mid-head and the (B,T,n_heads,head_dim) reshape at model.py:728-730 would silently scramble heads. Worth a one-line assert dv % head_dim == 0 (equivalently d_model % head_dim == 0) in validate_nested as defense-in-depth, since validate_nested is documented as the slicing-time gate.
evidence: Lines 235-237: '# n_heads <= supernet.n_heads is *implied* by d_model + head_dim being a ModelConfig invariant ... No standalone n_heads check needed.' validate_nested checks d_model<=supernet (231-234) but never d_model%head_dim==0; that divisibility lives only in ModelConfig.__post_init__ (177-181).
suggestion: Add an explicit guard in validate_nested: `if variant.d_model % variant.head_dim != 0: raise NestingError(...)`. Cheap, and makes validate_nested self-sufficient as the documented slice-time contract rather than transitively depending on ModelConfig construction having happened.
verify_note: Accurately scoped. validate_nested (config.py:223-261) omits a dv % head_dim == 0 check, and the reshape at model.py:728-730 uses n_heads*head_dim from cfg. However the claimed 'silent head scramble' cannot manifest today: sliced() (model.py:1192) always carries a genuine ModelConfig as variant_cfg, and ModelConfig.__post_init__ (config.py:177-181) makes it impossible to construct one with head_dim*n_heads != d_model. So the reshape last dim always equals d_model and heads cannot mis-tile. The finding itself concedes this is defense-in-depth against a hypothetical future bypass, not a current bug. Real but trivial hardening nit; low is correct.

title: Nesting is validated per-variant against the supernet, not pairwise across variants (small ⊂ base ⊂ large is unchecked)
description: _check_constants_nest_at_import validates each variant nests under SUPERNET, which is all the slicing code (sliced() always slices from the supernet) actually requires. But the design narrative (small/base/large as a strict ladder of nested slices) implies the stronger invariant small ⊂ base ⊂ large. That stronger property is never asserted. Today it holds (256<512<640, 768<1408<1792), but a future edit could give e.g. small a larger d_ff than base while both still nest under the supernet, silently breaking the conceptual ladder and any sandwich-sampling assumption that base contains small. Not a current bug; a missing guard against future drift.
evidence: _check_constants_nest_at_import (329-332) only loops `validate_nested(cfg, SUPERNET)` / `validate_nested(cfg, TINY_SUPERNET)`. There is no `validate_nested(small, base)` / `validate_nested(base, large)` chain.
suggestion: If the strict ladder is an intended invariant (it underpins shared-weight sandwich sampling where smaller variants are sub-blocks of larger ones), add pairwise checks ordered by d_model so a future dimension edit that breaks small⊂base⊂large fails at import. If only variant⊂supernet is actually required, document that the ladder is incidental.
verify_note: Confirmed that _check_constants_nest_at_import (config.py:329-332) only validates variant-under-supernet, never small-under-base-under-large. The finding's claim that sandwich sampling 'assumes base contains small' is overstated/incorrect: trainer.py supernet_joint_loss slices every non-supernet variant directly from the supernet model via sliced(model, spec.cfg) (lines 285, 311), never base-from-small. No code path requires the small-base-large ladder, so this is purely a future-drift / conceptual-documentation nit, exactly as the finding's own 'Not a current bug' framing states. Low stands.

title: rope_base nested-match uses exact float equality
description: validate_nested compares rope_base with `!=` exact float equality. The inline comment acknowledges this and justifies it (every config uses the literal 10000.0, so the bit patterns match). This is fine for the shipped constants but is a known footgun for any config loaded from JSON/round-tripped through a checkpoint config.json where the float could be re-serialized. Since run configs and checkpoint configs do flow through config.json (per CLAUDE.md), a rope_base that survives a JSON round-trip as 10000.0000000001 would raise a NestingError that looks like a real mismatch. Low severity because the literal is integral-valued and JSON round-trips 10000.0 exactly, but the assumption is undocumented at the checkpoint-load boundary.
evidence: Lines 254-257: `if variant.rope_base != supernet.rope_base: raise NestingError(...)`, guarded by comment at 250-253 'Float equality is safe here because rope_base is a default literal (10000.0)'.
suggestion: Either keep exact equality (defensible for an integral literal) but note the round-trip assumption at the config.json load site, or use math.isclose with a tight tolerance to be robust to arithmetic-derived rope_base values, which the comment already warns against constructing.
verify_note: Code matches (config.py:254-257 exact != with justifying comment at 250-253). Verified the checkpoint round-trip path: _cfg_to_dict uses dataclasses.asdict and _cfg_from_dict does ModelConfig(**raw) (checkpoint.py:230,247). rope_base=10000.0 is exactly representable in IEEE-754 and JSON round-trips it via repr, so the equality is safe for all shipped/serialized configs. The concern is genuinely hypothetical (only an arithmetically-derived rope_base would break, which the comment explicitly warns against). Documented-footgun observation, correctly low.

title: PRETRAIN_BUCKETS top edge must equal trainer max seq_len but is not enforced against MAX_SEQ_LEN structurally
description: PRETRAIN_BUCKETS = (256, 384, MAX_SEQ_LEN) carries a documented hard invariant ('The top edge MUST equal the trainer's max seq_len') but it is expressed only in a comment, and the tuple is consumed by the trainer. The last element here is MAX_SEQ_LEN so it is correct today, but there is no assert binding the top bucket edge to MAX_SEQ_LEN, nor that the edges are strictly ascending. A future hand-edit to a literal (e.g. (256, 512, 384)) would violate the ascending/top-edge contract silently and only surface as a trainer bucketing bug. This is tangential to the slicing contract but lives in this file's import-time validation scope.
evidence: Lines 122-124 comment 'The top edge MUST equal the trainer's max seq_len (typically MAX_SEQ_LEN).' followed by `PRETRAIN_BUCKETS: Final[tuple[int, ...]] = (256, 384, MAX_SEQ_LEN)` with no runtime assertion of ascending order or top==MAX_SEQ_LEN.
suggestion: Add a tiny import-time check (alongside _check_constants_nest_at_import) asserting PRETRAIN_BUCKETS is strictly ascending and, when non-empty, buckets[-1] == MAX_SEQ_LEN. Keeps the documented invariant from drifting.
verify_note: The missing import-time assertion is real (config.py:135 has no ascending/top-edge guard). But the finding's failure model -- that a bad edit 'silently surfaces as a trainer bucketing bug' -- is refuted by consumer-side mitigations. scripts/train_jax.py:304-307 filters edges to e<=cfg.seq_len and force-appends cfg.seq_len as the top edge, so a dropped/reordered top edge is self-healed. Corpus.by_bucket (corpus.py:122-132) re-sorts via sorted(set(edges)) and raises a LOUD ValueError if the top edge != corpus seq_len. So (256,512,384) would be re-sorted, not silently mis-bucketed, and a genuine top-edge mismatch raises rather than corrupts. The 'silent' qualifier is wrong; the check would be redundant convenience. Low (borderline none as a bug).

title: Logged train loss in stochastic-sandwich mode is the scaled estimator, not the deterministic sum — different magnitude and higher variance than --no-stochastic-variants
description: In the stochastic regime the returned loss is supernet_CE + N*sampled_variant_CE, which is an unbiased estimator of the full sum (correct for gradients) but whose per-step value is scaled up by N on the variant term and is noisy. scripts/train_jax.py logs this value directly as `loss`. Because stochastic sampling is ON by default (H.1), the default loss curve has a systematically different scale and much higher step-to-step variance than the deterministic sum a parity/debug run produces, even though the expectations match. This is easy to misread as instability or as a magnitude bug when comparing a default run against a --no-stochastic-variants run. Correctness of the optimizer is unaffected; this is purely an interpretability/observability concern.
evidence: Stochastic path: `... cross_entropy_loss(sub, batch, ...) * jnp.float32(n_other)` (line 316) then `total = total + sampled`. train_jax.py:473 logs `loss=float(chunk_losses_np[i])` with no annotation of the regime. With N=2 non-supernet variants, the variant term is doubled per step.
suggestion: Either log an additional debiased/normalised loss field, tag the metric with the regime (e.g. stochastic=True in the JSONL record), or divide the sampled term differently for logging vs. gradient. At minimum document in the dashboard that stochastic-mode loss magnitude is not comparable to deterministic-mode loss.
verify_note: Verified. trainer.py:316 multiplies the sampled non-supernet variant CE by `jnp.float32(n_other)` and adds it to the supernet term (325). This is an unbiased estimator of the deterministic full sum (correct for gradient expectation), but the per-step logged value is scaled up on the variant term and noisier. The deterministic path (280-291) sums all variants un-scaled. train_jax.py logs this value as `loss` with no regime annotation. With stochastic sampling ON by default, the default loss curve is systematically a different magnitude and higher variance than a --no-stochastic-variants run. This is purely an observability/interpretability concern; optimizer correctness is unaffected. Low is correct.

title: Resume resets PRNG key to key(0) and persists only {step}; checkpoint format docstring claims scheduler+rng are saved
description: scripts/train_jax.py:426 writes training_state={"step": int(state.step)} only, and load_resume_state (pawn/lifecycle.py:381-447) passes key=jax.random.key(0) — the same key as a fresh run. Variant-sampling determinism survives because the per-step key is fold_in(state.key, state.step) and step is restored, so post-resume keys continue distinctly; but this is incidental, not designed. The CLAUDE.md / checkpoint.py:19 format spec advertises training_state.json as {step, scheduler, rng (base64)}, and trainer.py's own module docstring lists `key` as part of TrainState; neither the key nor any scheduler/rng state is actually persisted. If the per-step key derivation ever changes to advance state.key (e.g. split instead of fold_in-on-step), resume determinism would silently break. Separately, the data-stream RNG np.random.default_rng(0) (train_jax.py:294) re-seeds to 0 on resume, so the random-game corpus restarts from the beginning rather than continuing.
evidence: train_jax.py:426 `training_state={"step": int(state.step)}`; lifecycle.py:447 `key=key` where key=jax.random.key(0) is passed from train_jax.py:231; checkpoint.py:19 docstring `training_state.json (optional) — {"step", "scheduler", "rng"}`; train_jax.py:294 `rng = np.random.default_rng(0)`.
suggestion: Persist the PRNG key (base64 of the key bytes) in training_state.json and restore it in load_resume_state, matching the documented format; or update the docstrings to state that only step is persisted and that variant-sampling/data RNG restart on resume. Make the resume RNG behavior explicit and tested rather than relying on fold_in(key,step) coincidentally preserving distinctness.
verify_note: Verified all sub-claims. train_jax.py:426 writes `training_state={"step": int(state.step)}` only. lifecycle.py:381-448 reads only `step` from training_state.json (409) and sets `key=key` (447), where key is the jax.random.key(0) passed from train_jax.py:231/242. checkpoint.py docstring advertises `training_state.json (optional) — {"step", "scheduler", "rng"}` — scheduler and rng are NOT persisted. trainer.py module docstring (line 13-14) lists `key` as a TrainState field, but it's not saved. The per-step variant-sampling key is fold_in(state.key, state.step) (trainer.py:813) and step IS restored, so determinism survives incidentally; if the derivation ever advanced state.key (split instead of fold_in) this would silently break. Separately, train_jax.py:294 `rng = np.random.default_rng(0)` is unconditional, so the random-game data stream restarts from seed 0 on resume. All factual claims hold. Low is appropriate: the documented format overstates what's persisted, and resume determinism rests on an undocumented coincidence, but current behavior is not actually broken.

title: make_scan_step wraps an already-filter_jit'd train_step, so train_step's @eqx.filter_jit(donate='all') is dead
description: train_step is decorated @eqx.filter_jit(donate='all') (line 808) but its only callers are the scan bodies inside scan_step / scan_step_with_norms, which are themselves @eqx.filter_jit(donate='all') (lines 908, 924). A jitted callee invoked inside an outer jit is inlined and its donation directives are ignored, so the inner jit and its donate='all' contribute nothing at runtime and add trace-time overhead/confusion. There is no path that calls train_step outside a scan wrapper (grep confirms). This is harmless functionally but the inner decorator misleadingly suggests train_step is independently donating/aliasing its inputs.
evidence: trainer.py:808 `@eqx.filter_jit(donate="all")` on train_step; trainer.py:915 and :931 call train_step from inside scan bodies that are also filter_jit(donate='all'). grep for `train_step(` shows only the two scan-body call sites.
suggestion: Drop the @eqx.filter_jit decorator on the inner train_step (leave it a plain function) since it's only ever traced inside the jitted scan; keep the jit on the scan_step wrappers. This removes the misleading donation directive and one redundant compilation layer.
verify_note: Verified. trainer.py:808 decorates train_step with `@eqx.filter_jit(donate="all")`. Its only call sites are inside the scan bodies at 915 and 931, which live in scan_step_with_norms (908) and scan_step (924), both themselves `@eqx.filter_jit(donate="all")`. grep for `train_step(` confirms no caller outside the two scan bodies (878 is `return train_step`, 887 is a type annotation). A jitted callee invoked inside an outer jit is inlined; the inner jit and its donate='all' contribute nothing at runtime and the donation directive is misleading. Harmless functionally. Low is correct.

title: seq_len has no upper bound against the model's max_seq_len (RoPE table size)
description: seq_len defaults to 512 and the only validator is seq_len > 0 (_check_positive_training_dims). The model is built from SUPERNET/TINY_SUPERNET whose max_seq_len is fixed at MAX_SEQ_LEN=512 (config.py:112,164,277,306), and RoPE cos/sin tables are built sized to cfg.max_seq_len (model.py:_build_rope, shape (max_seq_len, head_dim//2)). Nothing clamps cfg.seq_len to <= the model's max_seq_len. Passing --seq-len 1024 passes config validation but feeds T=1024 tensors into a model whose RoPE/position tables only cover 512, producing an out-of-bounds slice / shape error deep in the forward at first step rather than a clean config-time rejection.
evidence: run_config.py:281-282 `if self.seq_len <= 0: raise ValueError(...)` is the only seq_len check; config.py:112 `MAX_SEQ_LEN: Final[int] = 512`; model.py:226 RoPE returns shape `(max_seq_len, head_dim // 2)`; train_jax.py builds the model via init_model(supernet_cfg) with supernet_cfg.max_seq_len==512.
suggestion: Add a validator (or a check at script entry against the resolved supernet_cfg.max_seq_len) rejecting seq_len > max_seq_len with an explicit message, since seq_len > 512 can never work with the fixed-size RoPE tables.
verify_note: The capability gap is real: _check_positive_training_dims only enforces seq_len>0 (run_config.py:281); nothing rejects seq_len>max_seq_len at parse time, and train_jax.py never compares cfg.seq_len to supernet_cfg.max_seq_len. BUT the finder's failure mechanism is wrong. RoPE is NOT a fixed (max_seq_len, head_dim//2) table sliced at forward — model.py:565 rebuilds it per call sized to the actual T (_build_rope(head_dim, T, rope_base)). And model.py:553-558 has an explicit guard: 'if T > self.cfg.max_seq_len: raise ValueError(...)'. So --seq-len 1024 fails with a clean, specific ValueError at first trace, not an 'out-of-bounds slice deep in the forward'. The only defect is config-time-vs-trace-time error locality plus a missing clamp; it fails loudly and safely. Downgrade high -> low.

title: val_every is required-positive-validated but read by no trainer
description: val_every is declared on AdapterConfig (447) and SpecializedCLMConfig (643) and enforced positive in _check_adapter_cadence / _check_cadence. No code anywhere reads val_every: the adapter trainer keys validation cadence on eval_interval = cfg.eval_interval or cfg.log_interval (train_jax_adapter.py:543), and the pretrain trainer reads neither. A repo-wide grep for val_every outside run_config.py returns nothing. Users setting val_every expecting to control eval frequency get no effect.
evidence: run_config.py:447 `val_every: int = 1`; :546-549 validates it; `grep -rn val_every pawn/ scripts/ | grep -v run_config.py` returns nothing; train_jax_adapter.py:543 `eval_interval = cfg.eval_interval or cfg.log_interval`.
suggestion: Wire val_every into the adapter/CLM eval cadence (it is the natural per-epoch eval knob) or remove the field and its validators; keeping a validated-but-ignored field is a maintenance trap.
verify_note: Confirmed: val_every is declared (run_config.py:447,644) and positivity-validated (_check_adapter_cadence:546, _check_cadence:699) but read by no trainer. Adapter eval cadence keys on 'eval_interval = cfg.eval_interval or cfg.log_interval' (train_jax_adapter.py:543); pretrain reads neither. Grep confirms no consumer outside run_config.py. Real but pure maintainability/dead-knob trap with no correctness consequence (a value just has no effect). Downgrade medium -> low to match impact.

title: warmup_steps override is not validated non-negative
description: warmup_steps (explicit override of warmup_frac) is int | None with no positivity validation in _check_positive_training_dims, unlike total_steps/k/batch_size/etc. A negative warmup_steps would pass config validation; trainer._warmup_steps uses it directly (trainer.py:343 `cfg.warmup_steps if cfg.warmup_steps is not None`) and only checks warmup > total_steps, not warmup < 0, so a negative warmup feeds optax schedule constructors with a negative warmup length.
evidence: run_config.py:99-101 `warmup_steps: int | None = None`; _check_positive_training_dims (281-307) checks seq_len/k/max_corpus_gb/batch_size/total_steps/val_games/log_interval/weight_decay/lr but not warmup_steps; trainer.py:343-349 only guards warmup > total_steps.
suggestion: Add `if self.warmup_steps is not None and self.warmup_steps < 0: raise ValueError(...)` to _check_positive_training_dims.
verify_note: Confirmed. warmup_steps (run_config.py:101) is not in _check_positive_training_dims (281-307). trainer._warmup_steps (trainer.py:343) uses cfg.warmup_steps directly and only guards 'warmup > total_steps' (:346), never warmup<0. A negative warmup_steps passes config validation and would feed a negative warmup length into optax schedule builders. Note warmup_FRAC is bounded to [0,1] by _check_lr_schedule_fractions, but the explicit step override is the unguarded path the finder identifies. Genuine missing guard; low severity (requires deliberately passing a negative).

title: eval_interval / patience / pause_after_steps lack positivity validation and are mostly unused
description: patience, eval_interval, and pause_after_steps (all int | None) have no positivity validators and are not read by the pretrain trainer (train_jax.py reads none of them; see the cfg.* read inventory). eval_interval is read only by the adapter script as `cfg.eval_interval or cfg.log_interval`, so eval_interval=0 is silently swallowed by the `or` (falls back to log_interval) and a negative value would produce a negative modulus base in `final_step % eval_interval`. patience/pause_after_steps appear unused outside dashboard/benchmark tooling.
evidence: run_config.py:113-116 declare these with no validator; train_jax.py cfg.* inventory contains none of patience/pause_after_steps/eval_interval; train_jax_adapter.py:543 `eval_interval = cfg.eval_interval or cfg.log_interval`.
suggestion: Add positivity guards for any of these that are live, and remove or wire up the ones (patience, pause_after_steps) that no v2 trainer consumes.
verify_note: Confirmed with nuance. eval_interval/patience/pause_after_steps (run_config.py:113-116) have no positivity validators. pause_after_steps has ZERO consumers anywhere (grep returns only the declaration). patience is read only by the dashboard/model-card tooling for display, not by any v2 trainer. eval_interval is live only in the adapter path as 'cfg.eval_interval or cfg.log_interval' (train_jax_adapter.py:543) — so eval_interval=0 is silently swallowed by the 'or' (falls back to log_interval) and a negative value yields a negative modulus base in 'final_step % eval_interval'. All true; it is a grab-bag of minor maintainability/validation gaps. Low is right.

title: optimizer field comment advertises adafactor but the Literal forbids it
description: OptimizerName is Literal['adamw', 'lion'] (line 63, with a clear explanation at 57-62 that Adafactor is intentionally not wired). But the field-level comment at 92-95 says 'optimizer choice — "adamw" (default), "lion", or "adafactor"', advertising a value that extra=forbid/Literal will reject at parse time. Misleading to anyone reading the field doc rather than the type alias.

title: k docstring claims val cadence bounds K for adapter runs, but adapters never use k
description: The k field comment states 'Validation cadence bounds K for adapter runs (K ≤ val_every would otherwise drop val checkpoints).' The adapter trainer does not use k for any lax.scan inner loop — it loops step-by-step in Python (train_jax_adapter.py:209 parses --k but the chunked driver _run_steps does not consume it for an inner scan), and there is no validator enforcing k ≤ val_every. The comment describes a constraint that neither holds nor is enforced for adapters.
evidence: run_config.py:184-188 k comment references val_every bound; no validator in run_config.py couples k and val_every; train_jax_adapter.py:209 `ap.add_argument("--k", ...)` but _run_steps iterates `range(n_steps)` without k.
suggestion: Correct the k comment to reflect that k is the pretrain lax.scan inner length only, and remove the false adapter-cadence claim (or add the validator if the constraint is intended).

No validator in run_config.py couples k and val_every. The adapter trainer parses --k (train_jax_adapter.py:209) but _run_steps iterates range(n_steps) with no lax.scan inner loop and never reads k; k is only the pretrain scan-inner length (make_scan_step in train_jax.py). val_every itself is dead (see val-every-dead-field). The comment describes a constraint that is neither enforced nor applicable to adapters. Stale-doc, low.

title: generate_rosa_masks computes gradients for all adapter branches but only consumes sparse-delta grads
description: The Phase-2 grad_step differentiates the entire primed RoSAAdapter (LoRA A/B, sparse deltas, and the bottleneck branch when present) via eqx.filter_value_and_grad, then discards everything except grads.sparse.delta_*. XLA may DCE some of the unused-grad compute, but the LoRA/bottleneck branches are active in the forward composition (lora_active carried from init), so their gradients are genuinely computed and thrown away. Correctness is fine (the sparse-delta grads with all-True masks are exactly the Algorithm-1 quantity), but the LoRA branch participating in the forward during mask-gen also subtly biases which sparse positions look high-gradient (mask is generated against a LoRA-augmented forward).
evidence: _, grads = eqx.filter_value_and_grad(loss_fn)(adapter_); ... delta_grads = (grads.sparse.delta_q, ...) — LoRA/bottleneck grads in `grads` are never read; primed keeps lora_active=adapter.lora_active.
suggestion: Set lora_active=False (and bottleneck off) on the primed adapter used for mask generation so the gradient magnitudes reflect the sparse delta against the bare backbone (matches the v1 retro intent and avoids wasted LoRA backward), or document that mask-gen runs against the LoRA-warmed forward by design.
verify_note: Re-read adapter_trainer.py:401-486 and the caller (train_jax_adapter.py:587-608). generate_rosa_masks builds `primed` with lora_active=adapter.lora_active; the caller passes state.adapter straight out of Phase-1 LoRA warmup where lora_active=True, so the mask-gen forward IS LoRA-augmented and grad_step differentiates the whole RoSAAdapter (LoRA A/B, sparse delta_*, bottleneck) via eqx.filter_value_and_grad, then reads only grads.sparse.delta_* (472-477) -- LoRA/bottleneck grads are genuinely computed and discarded (XLA may DCE some but the LoRA branch is live in the forward). The efficiency waste is real but tiny (one-shot off-hot-path mask gen over mask_samples batches). The 'biases which sparse positions look high-gradient' framing is NOT a bug: I checked v1 (git show main:pawn/adapters/rosa.py:601+, generate_gradient_masks) -- v1 explicitly generates masks 'on a warmed-up model' and only toggles sparse_enabled/delta.requires_grad while LEAVING the warmed LoRA active. So mask-gen against the LoRA-warmed forward is the intended RoSA design, faithfully reproduced. Confirmed at low severity, but the correctness concern is by-design; only the discarded-grad compute is a (minor) inefficiency worth a doc note rather than a fix.

title: Module docstring claims eqx.partition(model, adapter_filter(model)) split but the train step never partitions; freezing relies entirely on grad being taken w.r.t. state.adapter
description: The module docstring and several inline comments describe a two-tier eqx.partition(model, adapter_filter(model)) that separates trainable from frozen and lets jax.grad DCE backbone weight-grads. In the actual code there is no partition of a combined model: the backbone and adapter are separate fields of AdapterTrainState, and freezing is achieved simply by calling eqx.filter_value_and_grad(loss_fn)(state.adapter) (backbone is a captured constant). The result is correct (backbone is never differentiated), but the documented mechanism does not match the implementation, which will mislead future maintainers — dispatch_filter is only used in the script to size the optimizer's init, not to partition the model.
evidence: Docstring: 'The two-tier partition uses eqx.partition to separate trainable (adapter) from frozen (backbone)'. Code: loss, grads = eqx.filter_value_and_grad(loss_fn)(state.adapter) — no eqx.partition call anywhere in the train step.
suggestion: Reword the docstring/comments to describe the actual mechanism (grad taken only w.r.t. the adapter PyTree; backbone closed over as a constant), and note that dispatch_filter's role is sizing optimizer.init over the trainable subset.
verify_note: Re-read adapter_trainer.py docstring lines 1-9 and 246, and grepped eqx.partition repo-wide: it appears ONLY in the docstrings/comments (lines 5, 246), never as an actual call. Freezing is achieved by eqx.filter_value_and_grad(loss_fn)(state.adapter) at line 273 (and 462 for mask-gen) with state.backbone closed over as a constant in loss_fn (line 266). dispatch_filter/eqx.filter is used only to size optimizer.init (script lines 398,412,617). The result is correct (backbone never differentiated; FLOP saving is real because backbone grads are never even formed), but the documented 'two-tier eqx.partition(model, adapter_filter(model))... XLA DCEs the backbone weight-gradients' mechanism is inaccurate -- there is no combined-model partition and no DCE step; backbone grads are simply never requested. CLAUDE.md repeats the same inaccurate description. Confirmed low/maintainability.

title: Backbone held as a JIT constant in AdapterTrainState but donated via donate='all' — frozen backbone is re-uploaded/re-bound every step and the donation contract is on data that never changes
description: make_adapter_train_step uses @eqx.filter_jit(donate='all') over (state, batch). state.backbone is part of the AdapterTrainState PyTree but is never updated (new_state re-passes state.backbone). Donating 'all' marks the backbone buffers as donatable each step even though they are invariant. Because the loop re-feeds the same Python state object (rebound each iteration to the returned new_state which carries the same backbone arrays), this works, but it (a) prevents XLA from treating the large frozen backbone as a stable constant and (b) means the backbone is threaded through the donate/alias machinery every single step. Combined with the no-scan loop (adapter-loop-no-scan), the frozen backbone participates in per-step donation bookkeeping it doesn't need. A cleaner design closes the backbone over the jit closure (like apply_fn) rather than carrying+donating it in the state. Not a correctness bug (verified new_state.backbone == state.backbone), but a structural inefficiency that compounds the missing-scan finding.
evidence: (surfaced by skeptic pass)
verify_note: Found by adversarial skeptic.

title: AdamW bf16 first-moment (mu_dtype=jnp.bfloat16) round-trips through safetensors.numpy but is never exercised by any test
description: make_optimizer builds the production AdamW with mu_dtype=jnp.bfloat16 (trainer.py:605) / Lion mu bf16 (613). flatten_opt_state does jax.device_get(opt_state) then np.asarray(leaf) (trainer.py:644-652), so the mu leaves arrive as ml_dtypes.bfloat16 numpy arrays and are handed to safetensors.numpy.save_file (checkpoint.py:326). safetensors 0.7.0 (uv.lock) does support bfloat16 via ml_dtypes, and unflatten_opt_state's _dtype_for rebinds the restored leaf to the template's bf16 dtype, so the path is plausibly correct. But every opt-state round-trip test (tests/test_jax_lifecycle.py:456,467,480,498) uses bare optax.adamw(1e-3) with the default fp32/None mu_dtype — none construct the optimizer via make_optimizer, and there is no bfloat16 leaf anywhere in tests/ touching flatten/unflatten. The single production-critical serialization path (bf16 mu -> ml_dtypes numpy -> safetensors -> reload) is therefore unverified. If a safetensors/ml_dtypes version skew or an environment without ml_dtypes bf16 support is hit, save_model would raise (or silently mis-store) only at a checkpoint boundary on a long run, not in CI.
evidence: trainer.py:605 `mu_dtype=jnp.bfloat16,`; flatten_opt_state trainer.py:652 `out[key] = np.asarray(leaf)`; test_jax_lifecycle.py:498 `opt = optax.adamw(1e-3)` (default fp32 mu), no make_optimizer / bf16 leaf in the round-trip suite.
suggestion: Add a round-trip test that builds the opt_state via make_optimizer (mu_dtype=bf16), saves through save_model, reloads via load_resume_state, and asserts the mu leaf is bf16 and value-equal. This locks the bf16-through-safetensors contract and would catch any safetensors/ml_dtypes regression at CI time.
verify_note: Verified the test gap is real. make_optimizer sets mu_dtype=jnp.bfloat16 for both adamw (trainer.py:605) and lion (613). Every opt-state round-trip test in tests/test_jax_lifecycle.py (456,467,480,498,552) uses bare optax.adamw(1e-3) with default mu_dtype; none construct via make_optimizer and none inject a bf16 leaf. The _bump helper at line 506-515 only touches float (kind 'f', i.e. fp32 mu/nu) and int leaves, so even the restore test never sees bf16. So the bf16-mu->ml_dtypes->safetensors->reload path is genuinely unexercised by CI. However, I re-read the path and it is plausibly correct: flatten_opt_state does jax.device_get then np.asarray (trainer.py:644-652) which yields ml_dtypes.bfloat16 numpy, safetensors.numpy.save_file supports it, and unflatten_opt_state's _dtype_for returns template_leaf.dtype for JAX-array leaves (trainer.py:724-728), correctly rebinding bf16. So this is a pure test-coverage gap, not a known defect. Downgrading from medium to low: no demonstrated bug, only an unverified-but-plausible path. Suggestion to add a make_optimizer bf16 round-trip test is reasonable.

title: Atomic save never fsyncs payload files or the parent directory before/after rename
description: save_model writes payload files, the sentinel, then os.rename(tmp, final) with no os.fsync on the file descriptors and no fsync of the parent directory after the rename. On a power loss after rename returns, a journaling filesystem can persist the rename's metadata while the underlying data blocks of model.safetensors / optimizer.safetensors are not yet flushed, yielding a directory that exists with a .complete sentinel but whose payload bytes are zero/garbage. This is largely fail-closed: the next load re-hashes every file (verify_sentinel) and raises CheckpointIntegrityError rather than silently loading corruption, and the prior checkpoint is immutable so it survives. But the just-written checkpoint can be unrecoverable after a crash, and a HF push that races the flush could publish a corrupt blob. v1 had the same gap (no regression), and the safetensors header makes truncation likely to be caught, so severity is low.
evidence: checkpoint.py:341 `os.rename(tmp, final)` with no preceding `f.flush(); os.fsync(...)` on the payload files and no `os.open(final.parent, O_DIRECTORY); os.fsync(...)` afterward.
suggestion: Before write_sentinel, fsync each payload file; after os.rename, open the parent directory and fsync it so the rename is durable. This closes the crash-after-rename window and makes the integrity guarantee a durability guarantee rather than just a detection guarantee.
verify_note: Verified: save_model writes payload files, write_sentinel, then os.rename(tmp, final) (checkpoint.py:338-341) with no os.fsync on payload fds and no parent-dir fsync. The crash-after-rename-before-data-flush window is real on journaling filesystems. Mitigations the finder cited are accurate: every load re-hashes via verify_sentinel and raises CheckpointIntegrityError (fail-closed detection, not silent corruption), and the prior immutable checkpoint survives. v1 (main:pawn/checkpoint.py:~135-139) likewise had no fsync, so this is not a new regression — pre-existing gap, kept low. One sub-claim is weaker than stated: 'a HF push that races the flush could publish a corrupt blob' is not a real risk — the async HF push reads the local files through the page cache after save_model returns, so it sees the correct bytes regardless of fsync; only a host power-loss/crash leaves a locally-corrupt dir. Core durability gap stands at low.

title: final.exists() guard is a TOCTOU with os.rename onto a directory
description: save_model raises FileExistsError if final.exists() (line 287), then later os.rename(tmp, final) (line 341). Between the check and the rename a concurrent process could create `final`. os.rename onto an existing directory is non-atomic in effect: if `final` became a non-empty dir the rename raises ENOTEMPTY/OSError (surfaced, acceptable), but if it became an empty dir POSIX rename silently replaces it, bypassing the immutability guard. The trainer's contract is unique per-step paths so concurrent same-path writes shouldn't occur, but the explicit-overwrite-is-a-bug invariant the docstring advertises (lines 280-282) is not actually enforced atomically.
evidence: checkpoint.py:287 `if final.exists(): raise FileExistsError(...)` separated from checkpoint.py:341 `os.rename(tmp, final)` by all payload writes.
suggestion: Replace os.rename with os.renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE) on Linux (or link()+unlink, or attempt rename and treat any existing target as the error) so the no-overwrite invariant is enforced at the syscall, eliminating the window between the existence check and the rename.
verify_note: Verified the window: final.exists() guard at checkpoint.py:287 is separated from os.rename(tmp, final) at line 341 by all payload writes, so a concurrent creator of `final` between check and rename is not guarded atomically. POSIX rename onto an empty target dir silently replaces it (bypassing the immutability guard); onto a non-empty dir it raises ENOTEMPTY (surfaced). The finder correctly notes the trainer's unique-per-step-path contract makes this practically unreachable, and v1 was actually worse here (main did shutil.rmtree(target) then rename, intentionally overwriting), so v2's guard is a real hardening even if not atomic. Genuinely-real but low-impact; renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE) suggestion is the correct fix. Low severity confirmed.

title: _expected_shapes hardcodes 64/64/5 for factored-embedding tables instead of deriving from engine constants
description: _expected_shapes pins embed_src=(64,d), embed_dst=(64,d), embed_promo=(5,d) as literals. These are the chess-domain constants (64 source squares, 64 dest squares, 5 promotion pieces) and are correct, but they are duplicated here rather than referenced from a single source (engine vocab / model.py). embed_pad and embed_outcome use cfg-derived widths (n_outcomes) while these three are magic numbers. If the factored-embedding decomposition ever changes (e.g. promo count), this load-time shape check would either falsely reject valid checkpoints or accept mismatched ones, and the drift would not be caught by the SAVED_FIELDS==16 guard.
evidence: checkpoint.py:210 `"embed_src": (64, d), "embed_dst": (64, d), "embed_promo": (5, d),` — literals, unlike `"embed_outcome": (cfg.n_outcomes, d)`.
suggestion: Hoist 64/64/5 into named constants in pawn.model (alongside the embedding tables) and reference them here, so the load-time shape contract tracks the model definition automatically.
verify_note: Verified: _expected_shapes pins embed_src=(64,d), embed_dst=(64,d), embed_promo=(5,d) as literals (checkpoint.py:210-212) while embed_outcome uses cfg.n_outcomes (214). The maintainability observation is accurate. Important nuance the finder slightly understated: model.py itself hardcodes the same literals in init_model (model.py:1133-1135: (64,d),(64,d),(5,d)) and in the jaxtyping annotations (459-460) — there is no named constant anywhere, so checkpoint.py is duplicating model.py's own literals, not diverging from a constant. So the load-time check cannot drift in isolation without someone editing model.py too, but the duplication is still real and the centralize-into-named-constants suggestion is valid. Low/maintainability confirmed.

title: _model_to_tensor_dict assumes fp32 params; np.asarray on a bf16 PAWNModel field would mis-store
description: _model_to_tensor_dict does np.asarray(node) on each PAWNModel array field. init_model always creates fp32 params (pawn/model.py:1122-1139; bf16 is a compute-only amp_dtype), so this is safe today. But there is no dtype assertion: if a future path ever stored a model whose weights had been cast to bf16, np.asarray would route through ml_dtypes and the load path (_expected_shapes only checks shape, never dtype) would not detect a dtype change. The save/load contract silently assumes fp32 storage without enforcing it.
evidence: checkpoint.py:134 `tensors[path] = np.asarray(node)` with no dtype check; _expected_shapes validates shape only (checkpoint.py:163-169).
suggestion: Either assert each saved tensor is float32 in _model_to_tensor_dict (fast fail if an unexpected dtype appears), or extend _expected_shapes verification to also check dtype, making the fp32-storage invariant explicit rather than implicit.
verify_note: Verified: _model_to_tensor_dict does np.asarray(node) with no dtype assertion (checkpoint.py:134), and _expected_shapes validates shape only, never dtype (199-226). init_model always creates fp32 params (model.py:1122-1140; norms/pad use jnp.float32, _normal_init produces fp32), and bf16 is a compute-only amp_dtype applied via .astype(compute_dtype) inside forward (model.py:562,602,720-723 etc.) — the stored model fields stay fp32. So the path is safe today and this is a latent/architecture fragility, not a current bug. The dtype-storage invariant is implicit; the assert-fp32-on-save suggestion is reasonable defense. Low confirmed.

title: Stored game_lengths is uncapped vs seq_len, so by_bucket effective-length can exceed seq_len and silently truncate
description: `_pack_clm` caps the loss_mask via `capped_lengths = min(game_lengths, n_move_slots)` but stores the ORIGINAL uncapped `game_lengths` in the Corpus (line 281). For Lichess, `_pack_dataframe` only clips game_lengths to per-row token count, not to seq_len. Thus a game longer than the move budget keeps `game_lengths > n_move_slots`. `by_bucket` computes `eff = game_lengths + outcome_offset` and `searchsorted`; when `eff > seq_len` the index lands past the last edge, gets clipped to the top bucket, and the rows are sliced to `[:edge]` — the game is silently truncated and its `game_lengths` field stays larger than the data it actually contains. The bucketing invariant (eff <= top edge == seq_len, asserted in the docstring at lines 123-132) is violated for such games, and downstream consumers reading `game_lengths` get a value inconsistent with the packed/truncated tokens and loss_mask.
evidence: game_lengths=game_lengths.astype(np.int32)  # uncapped; vs capped_lengths used only for loss_mask. by_bucket: eff = (self.game_lengths + self.outcome_offset); bucket_idx = np.searchsorted(edges_arr, eff, side='left'); bucket_idx = np.clip(...) — clamps overflow instead of rejecting.
suggestion: Store `min(game_lengths, n_move_slots)` (effective stored length) as the Corpus `game_lengths`, or have `by_bucket` clamp `eff` to seq_len before searchsorted and assert no game truly overflows. Keeping the loss_mask cap and the stored length consistent removes the silent disagreement.
verify_note: The mechanical claim is real: _pack_clm stores the uncapped input game_lengths at corpus.py:281 while loss_mask uses capped_lengths (line 260), and _pack_dataframe (lichess_data.py:264-267) clips game_lengths only to per-row token count, not to seq_len. So a Corpus.game_lengths CAN exceed n_move_slots. HOWEVER the downstream-corruption claim is effectively refuted by usage: by_bucket is the ONLY reader of Corpus.game_lengths anywhere (grepped: all other game_lengths uses are independent engine arrays in generation.py/eval_suite/extract scripts, not the Corpus field), and by_bucket is called in exactly one place, scripts/train_jax.py:343, on generate_corpus output only. That path uses generate_corpus(max_ply=cfg.seq_len, seq_len=cfg.seq_len) with prepend_outcome=False (default), so the engine caps game_lengths at seq_len, outcome_offset=0, and eff=game_lengths<=seq_len=top edge — searchsorted side='left' lands the top game at index len-1, no overflow, the clip at line 138 is a defensive no-op here. Lichess corpora (the only source that can produce game_lengths>seq_len, and only if extracted with max_ply>seq_len) NEVER go through by_bucket; they are sampled by slice_batch (trainer.py:93-102) which ignores game_lengths entirely and reads the already-correct loss_mask. So there is no actual silent truncation or consumer-visible inconsistency in v2. Real latent footgun (stored field disagrees with packed width, and the invariant assertion at corpus.py:123-132 only checks edge==seq_len, not per-game eff<=top), but no live impact. Downgraded medium->low.

title: make_epoch_schedule (multi-epoch tiling) is exported and tested but has no production caller; adapter trainer uses unbounded random sampling instead
description: The module docstring frames `make_epoch_schedule` as the multi-epoch tiling mechanism (a plan-called-out feature), and it is in `__all__` and unit-tested. But no training script consumes it: the adapter trainer draws batches via `rng.integers(0, corpus.n_games, size=batch_size)` every step (scripts/train_jax_adapter.py:561), and pretrain regenerates fresh random corpora per chunk (scripts/train_jax.py). So the only multi-epoch correctness guarantee the module advertises — every game seen once per epoch, deterministic per-epoch permutation, resume-stable index re-derivation — is not actually applied to the finite Lichess pool. The with-replacement sampling that IS used means over-/under-sampling of games and no epoch boundary semantics, which contradicts the stated tiling design.
evidence: git grep make_epoch_schedule -> only lichess_data.py (def + __all__ + docstring) and tests; the only batch sampler in train_jax_adapter.py is `idx = rng.integers(0, corpus.n_games, size=cfg.batch_size)`.
suggestion: Either wire `make_epoch_schedule` into the adapter/pretrain Lichess loop so finite pools are tiled without replacement and resumes are deterministic, or remove it and its public-API surface if with-replacement sampling is the intended design.
verify_note: Grepped the whole tree (excluding tests): make_epoch_schedule appears only as the def, the __all__ entry, and the docstring in lichess_data.py — zero production callers in scripts/train_jax_adapter.py, scripts/train_jax.py, sweep, or lab. The adapter trainer samples with replacement via rng.integers(0, corpus.n_games, size=batch_size) at train_jax_adapter.py:561, and pretrain regenerates fresh random corpora per chunk. So the module's advertised multi-epoch tiling / once-per-epoch / resume-deterministic guarantee is genuinely not applied to the finite Lichess pool. This is accurate. But it is unused-public-API + with-replacement-sampling-design, not a correctness bug in code that actually runs (no epoch semantics were ever promised by the trainer itself, only by this helper's docstring). Downgraded medium->low (maintainability/architecture).

title: Per-row Python loop to build move_ids is O(N) host work on multi-million-game corpora
description: `_pack_dataframe` materializes `token_lists = df['tokens'].to_list()` and then loops over every game in Python to copy each ragged token list into the fixed-width int16 buffer. For the realistic `pawn-lichess-full` slice (potentially millions of games) this is a pure-Python per-row copy plus a full Python list materialization of all token lists, which dominates the one-time cache-build cost and holds two full copies in memory. The cache amortizes this across runs, but the first build is needlessly slow.
evidence: token_lists = df['tokens'].to_list(); ... for i, toks in enumerate(token_lists): if toks: move_ids[i, : len(toks)] = np.asarray(toks, dtype=np.int16)

title: Full-forward (use_kv_cache=False) path recompiles XLA at every decode position

title: Ragged per-game prefix_lengths mis-prefill short-prefix games (latent)
description: prefill_len is derived from clamped_pls.max(), and the post-prefill next_logits is taken at logits[:, -1, :] (= absolute position prefill_len-1) for the whole batch. For a game whose own prefix is shorter than the batch max, positions (own_pl+1 .. prefill_len-1) are PAD_TOKEN, and the 'next move' logits used to start its decode are read at the longest-prefix position rather than at own_pl. The first sampled move for short-prefix games is therefore conditioned on a PAD-padded context at the wrong offset. All in-tree callers (prefix_continuation_test/poisoned_prefix_test use np.full uniform lengths; the others pass no prefix) avoid this, so it is latent, and v1 had the identical prefix_end=max() structure (intentional-drop rule does not apply). But autoregressive_generate is a documented public API that accepts a per-game prefix_lengths array, so the ragged case is reachable and silently wrong.
evidence: prefix_end = int(clamped_pls.max()) ...; prefill_len = prefix_end + 1; logits_jax, cache = _forward_cached(tokens_jax, cache, jnp.int32(0)); next_logits = np.asarray(logits_jax[:, -1, :])  — single shared frontier for the whole batch.

verify_note: Verified at pawn/generation.py:253-271, 382-398. prefix_end = int(clamped_pls.max()) (line 271), prefill_len = prefix_end + 1 (line 382), and after the single shared prefill forward next_logits = logits_jax[:, -1, :] reads absolute position prefill_len-1 for the whole batch (line 387). For a game whose own pl < batch-max, sequences[i, pl+1 : prefill_len] stays PAD_TOKEN (only sequences[i, 1:pl+1] is filled at line 266; the rest is the np.full PAD from line 238). So short-prefix games' first sampled move is conditioned on a PAD-padded context read at the wrong offset, and the subsequent decode writes all games' next token at sequences[:, prefill_len] regardless of own pl — wrong absolute position for short games. Confirmed that in-tree callers avoid this: prefix_continuation_test passes prefix_lens = np.full(n_continuations, p) (line 571, uniform) and poisoned_prefix_test delegates to it; the other three pass no prefix. title: nvidia-smi/rocm-smi shelled out on every logged train/val record, not cached at process start as documented
description: The module docstring (lines 7-9) and the _add_resource_stats comment claim GPU memory stats come 'via a shell-out to nvidia-smi or rocm-smi cached at process start'. On a healthy GPU this is tens of ms of fork+exec per logged step plus _query_jax_memory_stats calling jax.devices()+dev.memory_stats() each time; on a degraded driver each record can stall up to 2s while the training thread blocks. The cost is gated by log_interval (train_jax.py:467) so it is not literally every step, but it is every logged record and the docstring overstates the caching.

suggestion: Cache the smi numbers with a short TTL (e.g. refresh at most once every N seconds via a monotonic-clock gate) or sample them on a background thread, and correct the docstring/comment which currently claims the shell-out is 'cached at process start'. The JAX allocator stats (memory_stats) are cheap and can stay per-record.

The actual query path `_query_gpu_stats()` (line 290-298) dispatches to `_query_nvidia_smi`/`_query_rocm_smi`, each of which calls `subprocess.check_output([... ], timeout=2.0)` (lines 222-232, 258-264) with no caching/TTL. `_add_resource_stats` calls `_query_gpu_stats()` unconditionally for every include_resources record (line 562), and log_train/log_val both set include_resources=True. The module docstring (lines 7-9) and the section header comment (line 191) claim the shell-out is 'cached at process start' — only the *backend selection* is. So the doc is genuinely inaccurate. However I downgrade medium->low: the call is gated by log_interval (default 100, run_config.py:115; train_jax.py:467, train_jax_adapter.py:565), so a fork+exec of tens of ms amortized over 100 steps is negligible against a K-step compiled chunk, and the worst-case 2s stall on a degraded driver is bounded and rare. title: RNG key not persisted/restored on resume; training_state.json carries only step, contradicting documented format

For the model-init/stochastic-variant stream this happens to be safe because sub_key = fold_in(state.key, state.step) is keyed on the spliced step with a constant base key, so the per-step variant draw is reproducible across resume regardless of history. But the data stream is driven by a separate np.random.default_rng(0) reseeded fresh each process (train_jax.py:294, 375 _next_seed) which is NOT persisted, so a resumed run replays the same engine-seed sequence rather than continuing it. The net effect: resume does not reproduce the would-have-been data order, and the persisted-state contract documented for training_state.json is not met (no rng field, no scheduler field).

I refute the 'data order' framing as a real correctness regression: the data stream is fresh i.i.d. random games from the Rust engine seeded by np.random.default_rng(0) reseeded per process, so replaying the seed sequence regenerates statistically-equivalent random games — there is nothing to 'continue', no learnable order is lost. Net: the only real issue is the stale documented contract (no rng/scheduler field). Low is correct.

title: Adapter step_time metric divides elapsed by absolute step, mis-reporting on resume
description: In _run_steps, step_time is `(time.time() - t0) / final_step`, where final_step is the absolute step counter (start_step + offset + 1). On --resume from step N, t0 is set this session but final_step starts at N+1, so step_time = (this-session elapsed) / (absolute step) drastically under-reports per-step time. The pretrain script does this correctly with `(time.time() - t0) / max(1, step - start)` where start is the resume step.
evidence: train_jax_adapter.py:569 `step_time=(time.time() - t0) / final_step` with final_step = start_step + offset + 1 (line 559-564). Contrast train_jax.py:474 `step_time=(time.time() - t0) / max(1, step - start)`.
suggestion: Track a session-local step counter (offset+1 since loop start) for the step_time denominator, or subtract resume_step: `/ max(1, final_step - resume_step)`.
verify_note: In _run_steps, t0 is set once per session at train_jax_adapter.py:544; final_step = start_step + offset + 1 (line 564) is the ABSOLUTE counter; step_time = (time.time() - t0) / final_step (line 569). On --resume from step N (non-RoSA path, start_step=resume_step at line 645), final_step starts at N+1 while elapsed is session-local, so step_time is divided by the absolute step and badly under-reports. Contrast the pretrain script train_jax.py:475 which uses (time.time()-t0)/max(1, step-start) with start=int(state.step) (line 431), correctly resume-relative. RoSA resume is rejected upstream (lines 319-327) so only non-RoSA resumes are affected, but those do hit it. Cosmetic metric mis-report, low severity, confirmed.

title: accumulation_steps>1 only settable via --config and raises NotImplementedError
description: PretrainConfig.accumulation_steps exists and make_train_step reportedly supports it, but train_jax.py raises NotImplementedError for any value != 1 because the bucketed prefetcher emits (K,B,T) not (K,N,B,T). There is also no --accumulation-steps CLI flag, so the field is only reachable via --config JSON and immediately errors. This is a partially-wired capability that's effectively unusable; the trainer-side support is dead from the CLI.

suggestion: Either wire the prefetcher to produce (K,N,B,T) and expose --accumulation-steps, or drop accumulation_steps from PretrainConfig until the data loop supports it so the field can't be set into a guaranteed crash.
verify_note: train_jax.py:259-269 raises NotImplementedError for any accumulation_steps != 1, with the explicit comment that the bucketed prefetcher emits (K,B,T) not (K,N,B,T). grep for 'accumulation' in train_jax.py shows no add_argument; the field is reachable only via --config JSON, where any value !=1 immediately crashes. title: AdapterObjective spawns 'python' from PATH rather than sys.executable
description: AdapterObjective.python defaults to the bare string 'python' and is used in subprocess.run. In a uv workspace the active venv's python is on PATH so this usually works, but it's fragile: a study launched outside an activated env, or where 'python' resolves to a system interpreter without JAX, silently fails every trial. sys.executable would pin the spawned trials to the same interpreter as the driver.
evidence: pawn/sweep.py:250 `python: str = 'python'`; line 264 `self.python, self.script, ...` passed to subprocess.run.
suggestion: Default `python` to sys.executable (still overridable). Keeps trials on the same interpreter/venv as the Optuna driver.
verify_note: pawn/sweep.py:250 AdapterObjective.python defaults to the literal 'python' and is used at line 264 in the subprocess.run cmd. If the study is launched from an interpreter where bare 'python' on PATH differs from the driver's interpreter (e.g. not in an activated venv, or a system python without JAX), every trial silently fails (TrialPruned via returncode). sys.executable would pin trials to the driver's interpreter. Real but low-severity maintainability/robustness concern; in the documented `uv run` workflow it usually resolves correctly. Confirmed.
